title: The decline of ultramarine in manuscript illumination
bodyMd:
For most of the twentieth century, historians of manuscript illumination explained the decline of ultramarine in northern European workshops after about 1360 as a matter of supply. The pigment was ground from lapis lazuli mined in a single remote region, it reached the workshops only after a journey of several thousand miles, and the overland routes it travelled were badly disrupted in the middle of the century. When the stone became scarce, the argument runs, illuminators turned to azurite, a copper mineral dug from several European mines, which yields a greener and less stable blue at a fraction of the cost.

The account has the appeal of economy, and its premises are not in dispute. Its difficulty is that it predicts the wrong pattern. If scarcity drove the change, the workshops least able to pay should have abandoned ultramarine first and the richest should have clung to it longest. Tomasz Weller's survey of workshop records finds nearly the reverse. Several workshops attached to cathedral chapters, whose account books show ultramarine in stock throughout the 1370s, nonetheless used azurite for the skies and draperies of their most expensive commissions, while modest town workshops went on applying small quantities of ultramarine to the robes of the Virgin, where convention demanded it. Weller concludes that the change was a matter of taste: patrons had come to prefer the cooler, more varied surfaces that azurite, laid in several thin layers, could produce.

Weller's evidence establishes less than he supposes, though more than his critics allow. The account books he relies on survive almost exclusively from wealthy chapters; the town workshops are known chiefly from their manuscripts, so their stocks can be inferred only from what they painted. A town workshop that reserved its ultramarine for the Virgin may have done so not from attachment to convention but because it could afford no more, which is precisely what the scarcity account would lead one to expect. What Weller has shown is that at the top of the market ultramarine was being passed over by workshops that could have used it. That is enough to refute the claim that scarcity alone explains the change. Whether scarcity contributed at all is a question on which the surviving records are silent, though the likeliest history may be one in which a shortage first made azurite familiar and a taste formed under that necessity then outlasted it.

A town workshop that reserved its ultramarine for the Virgin may have done so not from attachment to convention but because it could afford no more, which is exactly what the scarcity account would predict. provenance.notes: Original passage written for wave 7 to carry a three-question Reading Comprehension set. Ultramarine, lapis lazuli and azurite are real pigments and minerals, but the historiographical dispute, the researcher Tomasz Weller, his survey of account books, the cathedral and town workshop pattern and every sentence of the wording are invented. The argument is deliberately qualified: the author concedes the supply account's premises and exposes a weakness in the challenger's evidence, which a reader can mistake for a defence of the old view, before concluding that the challenge refutes only the claim that scarcity alone explains the change. Not taken from or modelled on any ETS passage or any published article. Every fact the three questions need is stated in the passage.
